title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.

content_excerpt: Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. The overview shows how recommendation models generate item IDs or score supplied candidates. The OneRec-1.7B example below follows the generation path, from a viewer’s history to 128 candidate SIDs. A recommendation service has to turn a long interaction history into a set of candidates within a single request’s latency budget. Generating each item ID may take only a few tokens, yet the engine must explore many paths and return items the application can serve. vLLM-GR builds its recommendation search into the vLLM engine. vLLM supplies the scheduler, model execution, and paged KV cache. vLLM-GR adds a beam session that spans the whole search and keeps track of how candidate paths branch. EngineCore owns each beam session from admission to completion. The scheduler dispatches prefill and decode stages to a worker. At each stage, the model runner scores the next token and beam selection records the score and parent of each surviving path. The next decode uses those parent indices to read the right KV state. One request returns two candidates with beam widths of 2 → 3 → 2. The catalog filters out A1 · B1 because no item starts with that prefix. A full-vocabulary search skips this filter. The SIDs and scores are illustrative. In the prefill–decode–decode (PDD) pipeline, the scheduler admits a BeamSearch() request and dispatches its prefill stage to the worker. Prefill scores the first SID component while the host prepares decode 1. During decode 1, the host prepares decode 2. The second decode inherits the selected parents’ suffix KV and completes two SIDs. Green marks the component selected at each stage. The benchmarks measure P99 latency to show how beam width and batch size affect tail latency for generative recommendation. The two overview charts hold the input length at 1,024 tokens and compare beam widths of 256 and 128 at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8 across four NVIDIA GPUs and two Ascend NPUs. title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
summary:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.

It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.

I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.

Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.

It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.

I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents
summary: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.

title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?
summary: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.

title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokmål, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.

title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
summary:
Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control.
  On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. title: vllm v0.34.0
summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

title: Ultimate guide for fixing your team’s API keys
summary:
Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down. 

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage company, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

In our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:

  • Authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

  • Authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

  • Lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

Why a raw key is different

An AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the company, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

That is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:

  • A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

  • More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

  • You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:

Step one: Give each person one login

Each person on the team runs one command:

code_block

A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=my-startup-dev'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598d810>)])]>

Someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four shows how.

Step two: Call any model with that login

That single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need new accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google import genai\r\n\r\nclient = genai.Client(enterprise=True, project="my-startup-dev", location="global")\r\nresp = client.models.generate_content(model="gemini-4-hydrogen", contents="Hi")\r\nprint(resp.text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598f8d0>)])]>

enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from anthropic import AnthropicVertex\r\n\r\nclient = AnthropicVertex(project_id="my-startup-dev", region="global")\r\nmsg = client.messages.create(\r\n model="claude-sonnet-5-5",\r\n max_tokens=512,\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(msg.content[0].text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598fa90>)])]>

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import google.auth, google.auth.transport.requests\r\nfrom openai import OpenAI\r\n\r\ncreds, _ = google.auth.default(scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"])\r\ncreds.refresh(google.auth.transport.requests.Request())\r\n\r\nclient = OpenAI(\r\n base_url="https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/my-startup-dev/locations/global/endpoints/openapi",\r\n api_key=creds.token, # a one-hour token from your login, not a stored key\r\n)\r\nresp = client.chat.completions.create(\r\n model="openai/gpt-oss-120b-maas",\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(resp.choices[0].message.content)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598e110>)])]>

Two things to know:

  • Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

  • OpenAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Step three: Give your app its own identity

Your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

The good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud iam service-accounts create agent-runtime \\\r\n --display-name="Runtime identity for the app"\r\n\r\ngcloud run deploy my-agent \\\r\n --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/my-startup-prod/agents/api:v1 \\\r\n --service-account=agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \\\r\n --region=us-central1'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598ec10>)])]>

Keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Step four: Give each identity only what it needs

Removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

Calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-dev \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598c2d0>)])]>

For the app, grant it to the service account:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-prod \\\r\n --member="serviceAccount:agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598cf90>)])]>

It takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:

  • If your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

  • The repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

  • To stop new keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

Step 5: Put the remaining keys in Secret Manager

Some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets create stripe-test-key --data-file=-\r\ngcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding stripe-test-key \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598d1d0>)])]>

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=stripe-test-key'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598cdd0>)])]>

Live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google.cloud import secretmanager\r\n\r\nsm = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()\r\nresp = sm.access_secret_version(\r\n name="projects/my-startup-prod/secrets/stripe-live-key/versions/latest"\r\n)\r\nstripe_key = resp.payload.data.decode("utf-8")'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598fd10>)])]>

Reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one new version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

Then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

What the new setup gives you

Once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

A spend cap that pauses the service

Standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

You can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m bonus_spend_cap.create_spend_cap \\\r\n --billing-account 012345-6789AB-CDEF01 --amount 500 --dry-run'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598d610>)])]>

Know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

Set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

Guardrails on prompts and responses

As soon as real users can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

A sandbox for model-written code

If your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'config=types.GenerateContentConfig(\r\n tools=[types.Tool(code_execution=types.ToolCodeExecution())],\r\n)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc7d598f750>)])]>

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Someone watching for unusual behavior

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Your 20-minute checklist

For your team:

  • Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

  • Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

  • Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

For your app:

  • Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

  • Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

  • Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.
